In general, our priorities have stayed constant throughout the last years, a long-term approach in hiring and retention of our workforce, student academic success and closing achievement and opportunity gaps, and funding to continue addressing learning loss and attendance issues, student health and wellness, and safe and well-maintained facilities. and our crossing guards. Alignment between the budget and the new strategic plan will be key as we move forward for FY25. We look forward to collaborating with you in all of the months ahead until the final adoption of our budgets. I would like to turn this over for even more details to Dr. Anderson, our budget chair. I think you covered quite a bit, but I do have a couple of things that I want to place in this room for consideration as we have these two joint bodies together. This is a great opportunity

for us to obviously hear about the budget landscape to come, but I do want to elevate what I think has been on all of our minds, which is the J-LARC study and the fact that our schools, none of our public schools are being funded in the manner that they need to be. discussion as well. And that has to be met with some additional support. And while we do carry the burden of most of our funding coming from local dollars, that is just not a reasonable and that should not be our sole opportunity to fund the needs that we have as a school system.

I do want to put on the table, since we have everybody in the room, a conversation that this body has had in 2016 regarding the meals tax. We do know as of that time, almost every jurisdiction had either 2.5% all the way up to 10% in D.C., which is a meals tax. We can't continue to fund our schools on the back of our homeowners.

So I would definitely appreciate an earnest return to that conversation because we could be really strategic with those additional kinds of funding, with construction, with preschool. I do know that in 2016, when the original conversation was had, the estimate in terms of the revenue to the county was $100 million, with 70% of that coming to the schools and 30% for county services.

I think we need to really think about how are we going to diversify the revenue streams of Fairfax County, and hopefully we can begin that conversation in this joint body here today. So thank you again for this opportunity for this discussion. Thank you. And before I turn over to staff for their presentation, I do just want to highlight one thing because, and I was trying to get away from policy stuff to kick things off, But I will say, since the JLARC study was mentioned, there's a lot of people maybe watching this at home that have no idea what we're talking about.

And so just so people understand, this Board of Supervisors has been lobbying for, as long as I can remember, not only for a better return in state funding, almost to empty rooms, and I can remember doing it a lot of times myself, to empty rooms, and lobbying for JLARC to do a real analysis of public education, which took years to do.

And we are at a moment, because JLARC is the equivalent for our congressional people, the Congressional Research, CRS. And it's an entity that does an analysis of state programs, funding, and studies, and it is nonpartisan.

It has put out a report that says Virginia is approximately $1,900 behind per student in education funding, and all of our surrounding states, but most particularly Virginia, is behind West Virginia and Kentucky in funding for public education, which in essence means what the state has said is that if you want a high-quality public education system, you have to pay for it.

The problem is if you don't have an economy to pay for it, how do you pay for it? And so what Virginia has done by underfunding education is set up different school districts across the county with very different opportunities available to the public. And forever here in Fairfax County, this Board of Supervisors has said we will not settle for a second-rate public education system.

We know it is a driver of our economy. And because we have a strong economy here, we are able to support public education. The two cannot be divorced from each other. And so we really hope that a lot of effort is made in Richmond, that we press hard with our delegation when we meet with them.

I know you'll be meeting with them soon. We're meeting with them, I believe, two weeks from now, that we push hard on this issue because this is a moment in time. This study can either collect dust and be ignored, or this study can be acted on and Virginia can get ahead of West Virginia and Kentucky, which frankly should embarrass everyone who lives in Virginia when they hear these statistics.

And so that being said, I do want to thank our county executive and OPA because they have begun a very sophisticated perpetual marketing campaign through our Fairfax Forward portals through social media, educating the general public on this.

And I would encourage everyone to engage in that, to follow that, to link to it, to use the very sophisticated marketing tools that the county has out there to help the general public understand what it is that we're talking about here. Because unfortunately, what has happened over years is Richmond's been able to get away from addressing this issue because the common person doesn't understand it.

And we need to change that into the common person understanding exactly what we're talking about if we're to move the needle. And so I would encourage everyone to pay attention to that marketing campaign, to interact with it, to share it, to share the graphs, to share the statistics so that the general public understands what we're up against.

And I do want to thank our county staff for taking that on because it's a little outside of our normal county box, but it's important enough to us and to all of our county residents to be talking about that. And so I could talk about it all day. I promise I won't because we got a lot to go. But I do think this JLARC moment is one we can't afford to miss out on.

Then on the non-tax revenue side, investment interest. This is a category that really has fluctuated a lot over the past number of years, certainly with the Feds taking action to increase interest rates. It's really benefited us in this category. information regarding the police bargaining unit and SSPBA. On the pay side, we've included a 3% scale adjustment. This is really more market-driven when we've taken a look at the agreements that other jurisdictions have in place along with some of the pay increases that other jurisdictions have included. This is very similar to the market adjustments that we would typically include for our compensation packages. The agreement also includes a 2% cost of living adjustment.

There is a note that if we fund an MRA higher than 2%, that would be funded. We had proposed shifting to a COLA for these agreements rather than simply agreeing to fund the MRA since we didn't know what the MRA calculation was going to be when we first started these negotiations, and we certainly don't know what the MRA is going to be in year two and year three of the agreements.

So instead, there's a baseline cost of living adjustment included for police. We've also included merit and longevity increases as well as a new 10-year longevity step. When we took a look at where other jurisdictions fell and kind of mapped up our compensation, we could see that we were falling behind in the middle of the pay scale, and so we've included a 10-year longevity step.

There are some other provisions in the agreement, such as a full-day holiday for Christmas Eve. Through conversations with our public safety agencies, they noted that they have difficulty in scheduling because there's a half-day holiday on Christmas Eve, so we've expanded that to a full day. There's some incentive pay for those that are getting bachelor's or master's degrees for the police department, and there's some additional stipends in there as well.

There's always a partial year and then the full-year impact the second year. For fire and emergency services, as well as public safety communications, their agreement is different. We really were working with the unions to try to meet their priorities.

Employees were then slotted in that structure, which might result in a small increase. They were slotted into the next highest slot. Then there was a 3% scale adjustment on top of that. So it's a little more complicated talking about the FHIR and DPSC pay scales because it is a new structure.

We've also included education incentive pay for this bargaining unit as well. and then there's some funding in there for specialty training for some of the specialty units.
